The LSHR powder had a particle size distribution of -270/+500 mesh, while the Alloy 10 powder was -170 mesh.
The LSHR powder had about twice the oxygen pickup compared to the Alloy 10 powder.
Severe smoking was observed during EBM trials of the LSHR powder, likely due to the fine satellite particles.
The hand-sieved Alloy 10 powder exhibited poor flow and raking behavior, causing challenges in the EBM process.
During SLM trials, the 160 W melt condition produced the best-looking rods for the Alloy 10 powder.
Evidence of thermal cracking was observed for some SLM melt conditions of the LSHR powder, but not for the 160 W condition.
The temperature at the disk trim was around 700°C, while the temperature at the disk bore was around 400°C.
Powder cleanliness is critical for the performance of turbine disk materials, as non-metallic inclusions can negatively impact fatigue life.
Additive manufacturing may offer geometric flexibility, improved microstructural control, and the elimination of legacy tooling compared to traditional cast-wrought processing.
The higher refractory content of the LSHR alloy made it more prone to thermal cracking than the Alloy 10 during the additive manufacturing process.
The LSHR powder had a wider particle size distribution with more fine satellite particles compared to the hand-sieved Alloy 10 powder.
Further characterization and trials are needed to assess and mitigate any potential thermal cracking issues for the LSHR alloy in the SLM process.
The SLM trials for the LSHR alloy showed more promise compared to the EBM trials, but challenges remain.
